session: Session 1 - Defining marketing and the marketing process
bullets: Simplified definition: marketing = creating + communicating + delivering value. It is not just advertising: it also covers segmentation, positioning, pricing, channels, new product development.
Textbook definition: strategies and activities to acquire and engage customers, build relationships and create superior customer value in order to capture value in return.
Value proposition: the set of benefits a brand promises to satisfy needs. To deliver it the firm designs the offering (product), sets price, makes it available (place) and communicates (promotion).

Product: features, design and needs of the target segment. Price: willingness-to-pay and how to set it. Place: which channel. Promotion: awareness, interest, adoption, loyalty and campaign effectiveness.
The 4 Ps come after the marketing strategy (target audience and positioning) and rest on an analysis of the 4 Cs: customers, company, competition, collaborators.
Competitors: who are the primary ones and what form of competition. Collaborators: partners such as shipping, payment, IT providers that help deliver the product.
Company: strengths and weaknesses versus competitors, goals, culture, values. Customers: segments, target, unique position.
Course grading: in-class mini-cases 20%, final exam 40%, Marketing Challenge 40%, participation bonus up to ±2 points.
examTip: Be ready to identify the 4 Ps of a brand (e.g. Starbucks) and say why a good 4 P mix still fails without analysing the 4 Cs.

bullets: Decision-making unit roles: initiator, information gatherer, decider, buyer, user, gatekeeper. Roles may overlap or involve several people, so tailor messages to each.
Three models of consumer behaviour: learning model, economic model, EKB model.
Learning model: behaviour comes from drives, cues, responses and reinforcement; repeated positive experiences build brand preference and eventually loyalty.

Economic model: consumers are rational and maximise utility while minimising costs (money, time, effort). Perceived value = perceived benefits − perceived sacrifice. It neglects emotional and social influences.
Washing machine example: identical machines at $300 and $250: the shopper picks the cheaper one.
Buyer process: need recognition, information search, evaluation of alternatives, purchase, post-purchase reaction. A need is a gap between current and desired state (Maslow's hierarchy links needs).
Framing: people are more sensitive to losses than equivalent gains. A $10 early-bird discount feels better than a $10 late surcharge at the same final price.
Anchoring (irrelevant information) and availability (salient information) are biases from intuitive judgments; meet customers where they are.
examTip: Apply the five-stage buyer process to a concrete purchase, and give the framing example (gain versus loss) when asked about biases.

session: Session 3 - Market analysis, research methods and SWOT
bullets: Steps in market research: define the problem, develop the research design, determine information needs, collect data (secondary and primary), analyse, report and present.
Qualitative methods: direct observation or ethnographic research, focus groups (6-12 invitees), interviews. Quantitative: survey research, experimentation, secondary data analysis.

Surveys poll customers on satisfaction, preferences, willingness-to-pay, knowledge, using closed and open-ended questions. Know the question types: yes/no, multiple choice, Likert (1-5 agree), rating scale (1-7), ranking, semantic differential, constant sum (100 points).
Qualitative research is not concerned with numbers and is flexible; quantitative research gives numerical data and statistical analysis.

Experiment example: scarcity cue (Only 5 left) vs control, random assignment, independent vs dependent variable (purchase intention), t-test. Field test: POP signage in 12 of 24 stores with a baseline period.
Data mining finds patterns in big data: Target's pregnancy prediction score from purchase histories.
Secondary data adds insight, can verify primary data (diaries and stated willingness-to-pay are unreliable) and tells you whether test results generalise.

SWOT: strengths and weaknesses are internal to your company; opportunities and threats are external. Market growth is an opportunity (not a strength). Be concise, support with data, prioritise themes.
examTip: Classify a research method as qualitative or quantitative, and state SWOT items correctly: internal factors are S and W, external are O and T, and an opportunity is a favourable external factor, not an action.

bullets: Four bases of segmentation: demographic (age, income, gender), geographic (region, climate), psychographic (values, lifestyle), behavioral (usage rate, loyalty, occasion).
Where to start: if you already have behavioral data, mine it (Netflix path); if not, survey a small sample and project findings.

Behavioral segments are built from what, when, how people watch and engage (e.g. Weekend Bingers). Use age and gender only to describe segments afterwards; segmenting directly on them raises fairness and privacy concerns.
Survey-based segmentation: write 2+ numeric 1-7 questions, survey a sample, plot answers as coordinates, spot clusters, classify others.
k-nearest neighbours: a new customer is assigned to the most common segment among their k closest respondents (k = 3, 2 of 3 neighbours decide).
Targeting uses the Growth-Share Matrix (BCG, 1970): market growth rate vs relative market share (your share ÷ largest competitor's share).

Four boxes: Stars (invest to defend), Question Marks (invest selectively or exit), Cash Cows (harvest cash), Dogs (divest). For segments: attractiveness vs our strength or fit, giving Prioritize, Selective Bets, Maintain and Harvest, Deprioritize.
Checklist for choosing segments: size or growth, our real edge, profitability and cost to serve, resource constraints.
examTip: Classify a segmentation variable into the four bases and place a product or segment in the right quadrant of the matrix using growth and relative share.

bullets: Positioning needs to be clear, credible and coherent; it is differentiation against competitors in the customer's mind.

Positioning map from brand attribute ratings: rate brands (1-10) on shared attributes, survey ideal points, reduce dimensions with Principal Component Analysis to 2D, plot brands and respondents together, match each respondent to the nearest brand.
Ideal-point model: consumers prefer the brand closest to their ideal; distance = √Σ(respondent_i − brand_i)². The smallest distance is the best match.
Map reading: Hyundai wins the value segment, Volvo the eco-conscious segment; Toyota and Honda sit at the same point so their split is noise, not signal.
Sneaker activity: map 8 brands, circle an empty space and decide whether it is a real opportunity or empty for a reason (no viable segment).
Volvo owns safety: founded 1927, gave away the 3-point seatbelt patent (1959). Credible attribute earned by action, evolving to safety plus sustainability.
GEICO owns value: direct distribution cut agents, then entertainment (the Gecko). Price position earned in the operating model.
Positioning statement format: for [target] who want [need], [brand] is the [category] that [benefit], backed by [proof]. Single-attribute positions are durable but must keep evolving.
examTip: Write a full positioning statement and test it for clear, credible, coherent; explain why a gap on a map may not be a real opportunity.

session: Session 7 - Marketing mix: product and pricing
bullets: Asking consumers directly misleads: everything is rated important, social desirability, and stated intentions differ from behaviour.
Conjoint analysis (attributes judged jointly) forces trade-offs: select attributes and levels (4-6), design product profiles, collect responses, estimate part-worth utilities.

Full factorial: 3 prices × 2 batteries × 2 brands = 12 profiles; fractional factorial is a smaller balanced subset; choice-based conjoint is most common. Uses regression for ratings, logit for choices.
Outputs: importance weights, optimal feature bundles, price sensitivity, share simulation. Limit: too many attributes burden respondents.
Three product levels: core benefit (why the category exists), expected/actual attributes (table stakes), augmented benefits (differentiation and pricing power). BMW example.
Over-augmenting a product carries risks; consider at which level a retailer can differentiate.

Co-branding: LEGO and Shell was functionally logical but image-incongruent; Greenpeace's 2014 film made it salient and LEGO did not renew. Controversy spills over and the brand with more emotional equity loses most.
Price is what is charged; value is what a product is worth to a consumer (maximum they would pay). Basic pricing: compute cost, research customer value, study competition.
examTip: Place each feature at the core, expected or augmented level, and distinguish price from value when asked how to set a price.

session: Session 8 - Marketing mix: pricing math, placement and promotion
bullets: Information to start pricing: fixed costs (operating and marketing), variable cost per unit, then breakeven quantity (sales needed to cover fixed costs) or breakeven price.
Markup % = (selling price − cost) / cost. Profit margin % = (selling price − cost) / selling price (percent of the selling price).
Price elasticity = % change in quantity sold / % change in price. Below −1 is elastic; above −1 (closer to zero) is inelastic.
Value-in-use exercise: O-rings at $5 changed every 2 months vs every 4 months with $5,000 shutdown per maintenance; compute customer value per ring.
Distribution connects products to people. Strategic questions: how do you want to sell, and how does the customer want to buy.

Direct channel is owned by the manufacturer (no third party): when customers are large, sales are complex, or it delivers value. Indirect uses intermediaries for new markets, small purchases and valued assortment.
Channel design: distribution's role in brand objectives, which channel types, what intensity, which partners.
Promotion mix and advertising (Budweiser Super Bowl example); omnichannel strategies as a recent trend.
examTip: Do not mix up markup (divided by cost) and margin (divided by selling price), and know elastic means elasticity below −1.

session: Session 9 - Wrap-up: challenge deliverable and course recap
bullets: Marketing Challenge deliverable: Session 6 slides plus 4 additional slides (product, pricing and placement, promotion), due 29 November midnight on Moodle.
Product shown as 3D model, sketch or packaging; promotion as one video up to 30 seconds or two visuals (AI allowed). The class selects best product; 5-minute presentation.
Must show how the product solves a need or opportunity found in the market analysis (value proposition).
Recap analysis: 4 Cs, competitive analysis with PESTEL and SWOT; S and W only about your company, O and T external.
Distinguish opportunity from strength: your revenue growth is a strength, market growth is an opportunity, a competitor's gain in share is a threat.
Recap positioning: clear, credible, coherent; segments and unique position.
Recap three levels of a product: core, expected, augmented.
Recap distribution: direct vs indirect channels and designing channel structure.
examTip: Link every element of your final pitch back to the need identified in the market analysis; consistency across 4 Ps and positioning is what is judged.

session: Case study - Subway: problems with place, product and price
bullets: Subway (founded 1965, franchising from mid-1970s) was the world's largest restaurant chain by 2011 (33,749 restaurants) but struggled from 2014 against Jimmy John's, Jersey Mike's, Potbelly, Firehouse Subs, Panera.
Case question: how can CEO John Chidsey fix product, place and price issues?
Place: too many stores and market cannibalisation; 2,376 closures between 2016 and 2018; franchisees complained of stores opening on all sides of them.
Franchise system: low entry fee, royalty 8% of sales (among the highest) plus 4.5% for national advertising; franchisees must buy food from the company; development agents had conflicts of interest.
Product: quality problems and a step back in freshness.
Price: years of the $5 footlong (2008 to 2018) made customers unwilling to pay full price.
Promotion: Jared Fogle campaign (2000 to 2015), Live Fresh Eat Fresh (2012), Make It What You Want (2018).
US revenue fell six years in a row: $11.9bn (2014) to $10.2bn (2019).
examTip: Structure case answers by 4 Ps (place, product, price, promotion), cite figures from the case and propose fixes consistent with the diagnosis.
